newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian states prod Canberra on tax reform.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian states prod Canberra on tax reform.

text.p: Australian states on Friday sought to kickstart national tax reform, agreeing to replace state taxes on bank deposits with one tax on withdrawals.
The agreement, announced after a meeting in Melbourne of the six state premiers and chief minister of the Northern Territory, does not yet include Queensland state, which has no deposit tax.

"Premiers and chief ministers with the exception of Queensland have agreed to abolish financial institution duties (FID) and replace it with a reformed Debit Tax on a national basis if Queensland participates," said a communique.
The initiative is not expected to have a major impact on state revenues, a Victoria state government spokesman told Reuters.

However, the communique said it would encourage savings by scrapping the FID tax on deposits and the new Debits Tax would be structured to ease the tax burden on low-income households and small business.
Victoria Premier Jeff Kennett, the states' loudest supporter of national tax reform, told a news conference that the premiers hoped the move would persuade Canberra to pursue reform also.
"There is unanimous agreement amongst us all in terms of both the urgency and importance of reforming our dysfunctional tax system," Kennett said.

"Every week that this not addressed, it puts us as a country at a disadvantage. Reform is absolutely essential if we are going to relaise our full national potential and establish new and internationally competitive industries."
The communique urged Canberra to re-examine its approach to national finance sector taxes with the aim to making Australia a competitive financial hub within Asia.
"These reforms will boost the competitiveness of Australia's financial sector in the Asian region," the communique said.
"However, more must be done as opportunities top expand the Australian financial sector are being missed."
The Australian Bankers' Association cautiously welcomed the initiative but said it had yet to see the detail.
In Victoria alone, the FID tax accounted for A$319 million of annual revenues in 1996/97 (July/June).
The take in New South Wales state is even larger.

The proposed new Debits Tax would effectively combine the two state charges currently imposed on bank transactions -- the FID tax and another charge on withdrawals called the BAD (bank account debits) tax.

"This would look at combining the FID and BAD in one tax and it would put in a rate of up 0.1 percent. So you are talking about 10 cents in A$100 transactions in moneys moving out of accounts," Kennett said.
